lead: An engine test gives three raw measurements: torque at the shaft, speed of the shaft, and the rate at which fuel disappears. Every performance number in this chapter is built from those three. Torque and speed give brake power, fuel flow and calorific value give fuel power, and efficiency is one divided by the other. Mean effective pressure rescales torque by engine size, so a 100 cc scooter engine and a 10-litre truck engine can be compared honestly. Datasheets, test beds and the fuel-consumption maps manufacturers publish all use these same definitions.
prereq: You need: bore, stroke, swept volume and the difference between a four-stroke and a two-stroke cycle (see the topics on engine terminology and on four-stroke and two-stroke engines).

blocks.text: On the test bed only the shaft carries work out of the engine, so two quantities are measured there: torque T, the turning moment in newton metres (N·m), and speed N, the rotation rate in revolutions per second (rev/s). One revolution turns the shaft through 2π radians, so each revolution delivers work of 2πT joules.

blocks.where: BP is brake power in watts (W); N is shaft speed in rev/s; T is torque in N·m. If the tachometer reads rpm, use BP = 2πNT/60 with N in rpm, or divide rpm by 60 first.

blocks.text: Brake refers to the brake that loads the engine, so BP is the power handed to the outside world. The gas inside the cylinder pushes harder than the shaft delivers. The rate at which the gas does work on the piston is the indicated power IP, taken from an indicator diagram (chapter 5.2). The shortfall is friction power FP = IP − BP: rings on the bore, bearings, and the oil and water pumps. Mechanical efficiency is the fraction that survives, ηmech = BP/IP = 1 − FP/IP.

sections.h3: Mean effective pressure: the size-independent number

blocks.text: Torque alone cannot compare two engines of different size. Mean effective pressure puts them on a common footing. It is a fictitious constant pressure that, acting on the piston through the whole stroke, would produce the same work per cycle as the real, constantly changing pressure.

blocks.where: bmep is brake mean effective pressure in pascals (N/m²); V<sub>d</sub> is the swept volume in m³; N is speed in rev/s; n<sub>R</sub> = 2 for a four-stroke (one cycle in two revolutions) and n<sub>R</sub> = 1 for a two-stroke. Equating this to BP = 2πNT gives bmep = 2π n<sub>R</sub> T / V<sub>d</sub>.

blocks.text: Put imep in place of bmep, and indicated torque in place of T, to get indicated mean effective pressure. Then fmep = imep − bmep. All three are quoted in bar, where 1 bar = 10⁵ Pa. A naturally aspirated petrol engine reaches roughly 9–12 bar at peak torque; a turbocharged diesel reaches 18–25 bar. The factor n<sub>R</sub> stays visible in every formula, because forgetting it is the commonest error in this chapter.

Fuel power is the rate at which chemical energy enters the engine: fuel power = mf × CV, where mf is fuel mass flow in kg/s and CV is the calorific value in J/kg (lower calorific value about 44 MJ/kg for petrol and 42.5 MJ/kg for diesel).
ηbth = BP / (mf × CV) and ηith = IP / (mf × CV)

η<sub>bth</sub> is brake thermal efficiency, η<sub>ith</sub> is indicated thermal efficiency, both pure fractions (multiply by 100 for per cent). They are linked by η<sub>bth</sub> = η<sub>ith</sub> × η<sub>mech</sub>.

Volumetric efficiency measures breathing: η<sub>vol</sub> = mass of air actually trapped per cycle ÷ (ρ<sub>a</sub> × V<sub>d</sub>), where ρ<sub>a</sub> is the density of air outside the engine in kg/m³. A naturally aspirated engine at full throttle manages 0.80–0.90; throttling at part load drops it far below. Relative efficiency compares the real engine with the ideal one, η<sub>rel</sub> = η<sub>ith</sub> / η<sub>air-std</sub>, the air-standard efficiency at the same compression ratio (see Ideal air-standard cycles and their comparison). It isolates losses the ideal cycle ignores: heat transfer, slow combustion, imperfect valve timing. Equivalence ratio is φ = (F/A) / (F/A)<sub>stoich</sub>, actual fuel-air ratio over stoichiometric fuel-air ratio; petrol needs about 14.7 kg air per kg fuel, diesel about 14.5, so φ < 1 is lean and φ > 1 is rich.

sections.h3: Specific fuel consumption, specific power and the curves

blocks.text: Brake specific fuel consumption is the fuel bill per unit of work: BSFC = mf / BP, with mf in kg/h and BP in kW, giving kg/kWh; multiply by 1000 for g/kWh. Indicated specific fuel consumption is ISFC = mf / IP, and BSFC = ISFC / η<sub>mech</sub>. A good petrol engine reaches about 250 g/kWh near its best point, a diesel about 200 g/kWh because of its higher compression ratio. Specific power compares engines by size: BP / V<sub>d</sub> in kW per litre, and BP / mass in kW per kg. Turbocharging lifts both (see Supercharging: objectives, types and effects).

Three curves carry most of the marks. At fixed throttle, BP climbs with speed because more cycles run each second, then falls when friction and breathing losses win; bmep peaks at a lower speed than BP. BSFC is a U against speed: high at low speed, lowest where η<sub>bth</sub> is highest, rising again at high speed. Against load at fixed speed, BSFC is poor at light load, because friction is a nearly fixed tax on a small output, and best around three-quarter load.

examples.question: A single-cylinder four-stroke engine has bore 100 mm and stroke 120 mm. At 1500 rpm it holds a bmep of 6 bar and burns 2.4 kg/h of fuel of calorific value 43 MJ/kg. Mechanical efficiency is 85 %. Find the swept volume, brake power, torque, brake thermal efficiency, BSFC, indicated power and friction power.
steps: Swept volume: V<sub>d</sub> = (π/4) × D² × L = (π/4) × (0.100 m)² × (0.120 m) = 9.425 × 10⁻⁴ m³, that is 0.9425 litre.
Speed in rev/s: N = 1500/60 = 25 rev/s. The engine is a four-stroke, so n<sub>R</sub> = 2.
Brake power: BP = bmep × V<sub>d</sub> × N/n<sub>R</sub> = (6 × 10⁵ Pa) × (9.425 × 10⁻⁴ m³) × (25/2) = 7069 W = 7.07 kW.
Brake thermal efficiency: η<sub>bth</sub> = BP/fuel power = 7.069/28.67 = 0.2466 = 24.7 %.
Brake specific fuel consumption: BSFC = mf/BP = 2.4/7.069 = 0.3395 kg/kWh = 339.5 g/kWh.
Friction power: FP = IP − BP = 8.32 − 7.07 = 1.25 kW.
examples.answer: V<sub>d</sub> = 9.425 × 10⁻⁴ m³, BP = 7.07 kW, T = 45.0 N·m, brake thermal efficiency = 24.7 %, BSFC = 339.5 g/kWh, IP = 8.32 kW and FP = 1.25 kW.

import math

D = 0.100          # bore, m
L = 0.120          # stroke, m
N = 1500 / 60      # rev/s
bmep = 6e5         # Pa
mf<sub>h</sub> = 2.4         # kg/h
CV = 43e6          # J/kg
eta<sub>m</sub> = 0.85

V<sub>d</sub> = math.pi * D**2 / 4 * L
BP<sub>W</sub> = bmep * V<sub>d</sub> * N / 2
BP = BP<sub>W</sub> / 1000
T = BP<sub>W</sub> / (2 * math.pi * N)
fuel<sub>power</sub> = mf<sub>h</sub> / 3600 * CV
eta<sub>bth</sub> = BP / (fuel<sub>power</sub> / 1000) * 100
BSFC = mf<sub>h</sub> / BP * 1000
IP = BP / eta<sub>m</sub>
FP = IP - BP

print(round(V<sub>d</sub>, 7))
print(round(BP, 2))
print(round(T, 1))
print(round(fuel<sub>power</sub> / 1000, 2))
print(round(eta<sub>bth</sub>, 1))
print(round(BSFC, 1))
print(round(IP, 2))
print(round(FP, 2))

traps: A four-stroke completes one cycle in two revolutions. Using BP = bmep × V<sub>d</sub> × N instead of × N/2 doubles the answer.
The formula 2πNT wants rev/s. Feeding 1500 (rpm) straight in without dividing by 60 inflates the power 60 times.
Bar and pascal are 10⁵ apart. Convert bmep to Pa before combining it with V<sub>d</sub> in m³, or the power comes out 10⁵ times too small.
BSFC is usually quoted in g/kWh but the mass flow in mf/BP must be in kg/h. A factor of 1000 slips in silently.
bmep is a fictitious pressure that gives the work per cycle; it is not the peak cylinder pressure, and volumetric efficiency is about air trapped, not about power surviving friction.

quiz.q: Define brake mean effective pressure and state its unit.
quiz.a: A fictitious constant pressure acting on the piston through the whole stroke that would produce the same work per cycle as the real cycle. Unit: pascal (N/m²), normally quoted in bar, 1 bar = 10⁵ Pa.

quiz.q: Write the formula for brake specific fuel consumption with its unit.
quiz.a: BSFC = mf / BP, with mf in kg/h and BP in kW; unit kg/kWh, usually reported as g/kWh.

quiz.q: Why is bmep a fairer basis for comparing two engines than torque?
quiz.a: Torque grows with engine size: a big engine makes a large torque simply because its swept volume is large. bmep = 2π n<sub>R</sub> T / V<sub>d</sub> divides by the swept volume, so a 100 cc and a 10 L engine are put on the same scale, and a higher bmep shows better breathing, better combustion or less friction. bmep still rises and falls with speed exactly as torque does.

quiz.q: A four-stroke engine of swept volume 0.5 L runs at 3000 rpm and delivers 60 N·m. Find BP and bmep.
An engine has brake thermal efficiency 32 % and mechanical efficiency 0.85. Find the indicated thermal efficiency.
quiz.a: η<sub>bth</sub> = η<sub>ith</sub> × η<sub>mech</sub>, so η<sub>ith</sub> = 0.32/0.85 = 0.376, that is 37.6 %.

quiz.q: At constant speed, why does BSFC rise steeply as the load is reduced?
quiz.a: Friction power is nearly constant while brake power falls with load, so FP/BP grows and η<sub>mech</sub> drops. Since η<sub>bth</sub> = η<sub>ith</sub> × η<sub>mech</sub>, brake thermal efficiency falls, and BSFC = 1/(η<sub>bth</sub> × CV) rises sharply. Light load also means a weaker mixture and poorer combustion.

quiz.q: A two-stroke and a four-stroke have the same swept volume, the same bmep and the same speed. Compare their torques and powers.
quiz.a: T = bmep × V<sub>d</sub> / (2π n<sub>R</sub>), so at the same bmep, swept volume and speed the two-stroke (n<sub>R</sub> = 1) makes twice the torque of the four-stroke (n<sub>R</sub> = 2), because it completes one cycle every revolution instead of every second revolution. BP = bmep × V<sub>d</sub> × N / n<sub>R</sub>, so the two-stroke also makes twice the power at the same speed.

beyond: Not for the exam. Test cells compute these numbers live: a torque flange and a Coriolis fuel meter feed software that prints bmep, BSFC and η<sub>bth</sub> every second. Emission tests report brake-specific emissions in g/kWh, so the same arithmetic sits under emissions work. Search next for engine downsizing and fuel-consumption maps.
